# Chapter Nine — The Last Portion

The dining room of the Hôtel Léman kept the heat of the day the way old buildings do — politely, and all night. The tall windows stood open to the quay, and the lake had gone from gold to pewter, Mont Blanc a smudge of slate with the last light bruised across it. Overhead, the fan turned with the unhurried patience of old hotels. Half the tables were set, and everyone was pretending not to mind the warmth.

Inspector Lena Keller had the small table by the pillar, the one with a view of the whole room, because she had asked for it and because asking was a habit she had never seen a reason to drop. She was dining alone for the fourth night — the omelette, the carafe, the notebook closed beside her plate. Technically, Konrad Voss was why she was in the hotel at all: a commercial tangle that somebody upstairs wanted understood, and Voss was the knot in the middle of it. Watching him was her work. Everything else she noticed was habit.

She watched hands. She always watched hands.

The Voss table was the best table, the round one beneath the long mirror. Voss himself was taking up more room than his chair, as usual — a big man with a big laugh, and people turned to look at the laugh and pretended they hadn't. His wife Ilse sat cool and dark-eyed at his right, saying little. The lawyer Meller faced them, sweating through a good suit, laughing a half-second late at everything, and glancing at his watch the way men glance at weather they don't like.

She had registered the waiter the way you register a clock: by his regularity. White jacket without a wrinkle in it. He never wrote an order down. He poured before a glass was empty and said barely a word, and he had a stillness about him, the stillness of things that are wound. He watched the Voss table the way a sailor watches weather — constantly, and without alarm.

When Voss lifted two fingers, the waiter leaned in.

"Tonight we have filets de féra, monsieur. From this morning's catch. I'm afraid there is only the one portion left."

Voss, who had been planning the veal, straightened with the pleasure of a man being flattered. "The last? Then it's mine, before someone braver gets it."

Meller took the lamb. Ilse asked for a consommé and, when it came, took two spoonfuls and let it stand.

*The last portion,* Keller thought, *offered to the richest appetite in the room.* Coincidence. She filed it in pencil.

The champagne went round. Meller said, "Friday, Konrad. Sign on Friday, and after that the Riviera, and none of us ever has to look at a bank again." Voss laughed and began the story — the minister, the mountain guide, the rope — a story he had told a hundred times and knew exactly where the laugh lived. He had got to the rope when the plates came.

She watched the hands. Meller's plate was set down the proper way, from the left, quietly. Ilse's the same. Voss's plate was set down — and then the wrist turned it. A quarter turn, smooth as dealing cards, so that the fish and its lemon sat facing him exactly, composed, presented. It looked like ceremony. It looked like care.

She filed it with the rest. *He turned only one plate.*

Ten minutes later, Voss lost the end of his own story.

He laughed anyway, alone, and said, "Where was I?" and reached for his glass. "The heat," he said, to the room in general. He unbuttoned his jacket. Voss unbuttoned nothing. At his temple, sweat caught the candlelight. His hand went for the glass and missed, found it on the second try, and he laughed at that too, but the laugh came out thinner than the one before it. The waiter refilled his glass though it stood half full. He did not do this for the others.

"Too much sun, Konrad," Meller said, and looked at his watch again.

Keller found she had stopped eating. Her fork was still in her hand and had been for some time. Something about the table had gone a degree off square, the way a picture hangs wrong — and the wrongness was getting louder.

Voss's voice was thickening. The story circled back on itself, and his fork rang twice against the porcelain, a small bright sound that made heads turn and then pretend not to. And then, terribly, gently, he said to his wife: "You have been very patient with me, Ilse."

Ilse went absolutely still. Because he never said such things. And because something in his voice was already leaving.

He stood up. Stood because standing was the last thing he still remembered how to do. The chair skidded; his hand slid along the cloth, gathering it, and the two nearest glasses went over. His plate rocked, slid an inch, and settled, upright. Then Konrad Voss came down onto the parquet among the broken glass, large in the way dropped things are large, and the room made a noise like one held breath let go.

The pianist stopped. The silence where the music had been was the true alarm.

"Konrad." Ilse said it twice. The second time it was not a name anymore.

The maître d' materialised. A doctor rose from the third table and came at a run, cuffs already rolled. Someone said brandy; someone else said *fainted, it's the heat, it's only the heat.* Voss lay where he had fallen, and the doctor's hands were moving on him, and everyone was watching the man on the floor.

Somebody had to watch the room.

The waiter came out of the kitchens carrying iced water before anyone had called for anything. He gave the doctor the aisle, tilted the lampshade so the light fell better — and then, while a man died under the chandelier, he began to clear. Stacked Meller's plate with the fork laid on it just so. And his hand crossed the cloth toward Voss's plate, toward the fallen fish and the lemon and the turned setting.

Keller crossed the room at a walk. There was nothing left in it that running would mend, and something in it that needed watching.

"Police," she said, quietly, in the voice she saved for rooms like this one. "Don't. Leave the table. Everything
reasoning:
The user is writing a detective novel set in an old Geneva hotel. They want a dinner scene for chapter 9 where the victim is poisoned. Key requirements:
1. Real tension
2. A suspicious waiter
3. The slow realization that something is wrong
4. The detective noticing a clue
5. No chemistry details needed — just drama

Let me think about what makes a great poisoning dinner scene. Classic references: Agatha Christie's "Sparkling Cyanide," the banquets in her work, Dorothy L. Sayers' "Strong Poison" (though that's more about the trial), the tension of a meal where we suspect something but characters don't.

Setting: an old Geneva hotel. Geneva in the 1920s-30s? The user didn't specify era, but "old Geneva hotel" suggests something grand and old-world — brass, velvet, lake views, Mont Blanc across the water, waiters in white jackets, a maitre d', the sound of Lake Geneva, perhaps the jet d'eau. I'll keep it era-flexible or lean slightly period — I could ask, but the request is clear enough to write; I can make it read as a classic mid-century feel which suits detective fiction. Actually, I should be careful not to over-specify the era in ways that might conflict with their book. Let me lean timeless-classic: candles, silver cloches, an old hotel with history. Maybe mention the lake. I could leave era ambiguous. I'll avoid hard dates. Perhaps subtle period touches that could be edited out.

Characters needed:
- The victim: I need a name. Something fitting. Let's call him... a guest at the hotel. Maybe "Aldous Winterbourne"? That's very English. Or something European — Geneva setting, international guests. Let me go with something like "Viktor Hahn"? Or "Emil Vasari"? Hmm. The user will want to swap in their own names, so I should pick serviceable names and maybe note they can be swapped. Let me choose: victim = "Mr. Aubrey Sanderson"? Or "Herr Falliner"? I'll go with something like "Edmund Ravel" — no wait, Ravel is a composer, might be distracting. "Aldo Brenner"? Let me think: the victim could be a man with a reputation, someone disliked — that gives tension and motive atmosphere. "Maximilian Ehrlich"? "Konrad Voss"? I like "Voss" — sharp, Germanic, fits Geneva's multilingual milieu. Victim: Konrad Voss? Hmm, "Voss" reads well. Or make the victim a woman? Poisonings in fiction often target men, but a woman could be interesting. The user didn't specify. I'll go with a man — say, "Aurelio Voss"? Simpler: "Mr. Voss," first name maybe not needed. Actually giving a full name adds texture: "Konrad Voss."

- The detective: The protagonist. The user says "the detective noticing a clue." The detective should be present at dinner — maybe dining alone, or with a companion, observing. I'll invent a name but flag it's a placeholder: "Inspector Lena Marchetti"? Or keep it Swiss-adjacent: "Inspector Anselm Roth"? Geneva — Swiss, French-speaking. "Inspecteur Dorothée Reynard"? Hmm. Let me go with something neutral the user can replace: "Inspector Haller" or "Detective Marek"? I'll use "Inspector Lena Vogel"? Wait — Vogel and Voss too similar. Victim: Voss; detective: let's say "Inspector Anouk Delar" or "Detective Reb Lasser"? Keep it simple: "Inspector Delaunay" — French-Swiss. Or female detective "Inspector Marguerite Soland"? Let me pick "Inspector Lena Delaunay" — actually maybe simpler: "Inspector Adler"? I'll go with a female detective, "Inspector Léa Fontaine"? Hmm, could be too romance-novel. "Inspector Camille Duret"? I like "Camille" — gender-flexible, Swiss-French. Detective: Inspector Camille Duret? Or make detective male: "Inspector Aurel Brunner." Let me settle: Detective = "Inspector Lena Alder" — Alder is a Swiss name (Alder is actually more German; Swiss names: Meier, Baumann, Frey...). "Alder" works and sounds Alpine. Victim = "Konrad Voss." Waiter = needs a name too: "Stefan"? "Emile"? A suspicious waiter — I'll call him "Rudolf" or "Pavel"? Let me use "Emil" — no wait, too close to era-generic? "The waiter, Marek" — Eastern European waiter in an old hotel adds slight outsider suspicion (careful not to make it xenophobic in a way that reads badly — but the character's suspicion of the waiter can be the detective's bias, which could even be a red herring; that's actually clever: the waiter being suspicious but perhaps innocent is classic). Waiter name: "Pavel" or "Stavros"? I'll go with "Pavel." Hmm, or keep him mostly "the waiter" with a name tag: "his name tag read K. BRONNER"? Wait, K. initials. Let me do "B. Keller"? Fine details.

Other dinner guests to build tension: the victim isn't dining alone — poison at dinner suggests companions. A table of suspects is classic (Sparkling Cyanide). Options: Voss dining with business associates or family: a wife, a partner, a rival. I'll include: his much younger wife? A nervous business partner? Let me include a small party: Voss, his wife "Ilse," his lawyer/partner "Dr. Meller," maybe the hotel director dropping by. Keep the cast tight: Voss + wife + one associate = 3 at table. The detective dining solo at a nearby table with a clear view.

The clue the detective notices: This is important — it must be subtle, visual, and not chemical. Options:
- The waiter serving Voss from a different direction than the others (so only Voss's plate/glass was reachable).
- The waiter's thumb position on the glass — a skilled waiter wouldn't touch the rim... but that's hygiene, not poison.
- The wine: the waiter poured Voss's glass first/left-handed.
- The bread or the sugar tongs — Voss uses sugar in his coffee; the sugar cubes come in a shared bowl, but someone handed Voss the dish specifically.
- The detective notices the waiter changed gloves, or that Voss was the only one served the special of the day (e.g., sole meunière) — the waiter told the table the special was sold out except one portion, which he offered to Voss specifically. Ooh, that's good: the "last portion" of a dish steered to the victim.
- A detail: the waiter pours champagne but Voss's glass gets poured from a different bottle, or the waiter returns to the table an unusual number of times.
- The clue could be: the waiter wiping a specific spoon/glass with his service cloth moments before serving — again others used same items.
- A distinctive: Voss takes his coffee black, but the waiter brings him the milk jug anyway — odd.
- Best structural idea: the detective notices something about who touched what in sequence. Classic clue: the waiter serves plates with his right hand over Voss's left shoulder... but for Voss's plate he set it down and *rotated it* — turning the plate so a particular side faced Voss. Only Voss's plate got turned. Turning a plate could position something (a garnish, or a spot where something was applied). The detective later realizes: why did he turn only that plate? That's elegant, visual, non-chemical.
- Or: the candle/candlelight angle; shadows. Hmm.
- Or: the salt. Voss salts his food heavily; the detective notices the salt cellar at Voss's end of the table... others used it too though.
- The "turned plate" clue is my favorite. Alternatively: the waiter refills water glasses from a pitcher, but for Voss he fetched a fresh glass from the service stand instead of refilling. Also strong: inconsistency in service is the tell. The best clue should be small enough to miss in the moment but damning in retrospect. I'll use the plate rotation + maybe the wine pour order. Actually, let me pick ONE clear clue and render it precisely: the detective, watching idly, notices the waiter — smooth, practiced — turn Voss's plate a quarter-turn after setting it, and only Voss's plate. Or she notices him hold Voss's plate differently — his fingers on the rim vs the underside. Hmm, fingers on the rim for the victim's plate. That's nice: a trained waiter carries plates with thumbs on the rim edge; but the detective notices for Voss's plate his hand hovered differently... too fiddly.

Let me think about which clue reads best in prose for a lay reader: The detective sees the waiter set the plates, then — a small thing — adjust Voss's plate, turning it so the fish's head/tail or the lemon faced him. A quarter turn, done so smoothly it looked like care. Later she asks herself: why turn the plate? She measures the table, the angle of his approach. If the dish had been dosed at one edge... but user said no chemistry, so I don't need to explain the mechanism — the clue just needs to be *noticed*, and its significance left ominous. Good: "He turned only one plate." That's the line. The detective notices at the time it's odd but files it; then when Voss collapses, the detail detonates.

Also the wine: another possible clue — the waiter pours for everyone, but Voss's glass he fills last/from a different bottle... I'll pick the plate turn as the noticed clue, and maybe layer a secondary oddity: the waiter recommending the special only when Voss asked; or the way he positioned himself. Layering two subtle oddities (one noted, one noted lightly) is realistic — real detective fiction does this. But I must keep it clean: primary clue = the turned plate; secondary ambience = the waiter's over-attention to Voss, refilling a glass that was nearly full, or fetching a specific bottle. Hmm — over-attention is good tension.

Slow realization that something is wrong: The victim's symptoms should start subtle — user said no chemistry needed, so I'll keep symptoms vague and behavioral: he pauses mid-sentence, loses the thread; unbuttoning his jacket as if hot; his voice thinning; a slight slur he blames on the wine; his hand missing the glass; sweat at the temples; the joke he doesn't finish; then the fork ringing against the plate, the collapse, the overturned chair. I should NOT specify real poison symptoms (that edges toward how-to? No — symptoms of poisoning in fiction are fine and non-actionable; but user explicitly said no chemistry, so vagueness also serves the prose). I'll render it as the room's misunderstanding first: everyone thinks it's his heart, the heat, too much wine — that's the slow realization, first the reader/watcher senses it, then the wife, then the room, then panic.

Suspicious waiter: What makes him suspicious without cartoonish villainy? Best practice: he's *too* polished, and small wrongnesses accumulate: he doesn't sweat; he watches; he corrects a small error with eerie calm; he's new — "only three weeks at the hotel" the maître d' says later; he lingers; his eyes go to the detective noticing him; after the collapse he's the one who calls for calm/doctor efficiently, perhaps too efficiently; he disappears to the kitchens; he was near the table an unusual number of times. Also good: he never writes orders down, he anticipated Voss's order. The menace of competence. And a physical tell: a scar? no — subtler: he is left-handed? Hmm, careful: left-handedness + which hand touched what could combine with the plate clue. Could be elegant: he serves right-handed but the detective notices him do something left-handed later. Maybe too much. Keep: his stillness, his watching, the fact that when the room erupts, he is calm; he removes things from the table — oh! Key suspicious action: after Voss collapses, the waiter begins to *clear the plates* — reaching for Voss's plate — and the detective stops him. That's a classic and gives the detective an active moment: "Touch nothing." And it retroactively loads the plate-turn clue. Excellent — the scene should end with or near that beat: detective stopping the clearing, pocketing/noting the plate, the waiter's face doing something small. Maybe the waiter meeting her eyes — a flat, evaluating look — before he bows and retreats. And final line hook for chapter end.

Structure of the scene (length: user asked for a full scene; this is creative writing, so a substantial piece is fine — maybe 900–1400 words. Format: prose, maybe with a scene title. No headers needed beyond maybe a chapter marker. No bullet points — it's fiction. I could add a brief note after about the planted clue and how it can be adjusted, since the user is the novelist and might appreciate a short craft note — e.g., "the clue is the turned plate; you can pay it off in ch. 12 by..." That's genuinely useful for a novelist. Keep the note short, 3–5 bullet-ish lines or a short paragraph. A few sentences after the scene is appropriate and not over-formatting.)

POV choice: The user says "the detective noticing a clue" — I could write from the detective's POV (limited third) which makes the noticing natural: she notices, files it away. But tension trick: if in her POV, do we know the victim will be poisoned? Dramatic irony vs discovery. If I write from the detective's POV who merely dines nearby and observes, the poisoning unfolds as she watches — she doesn't know; she notices oddities; then collapse. That gives us both tension and the clue naturally. Alternatively omniscient dipping into the victim's fading perception — powerful for "slow realization something is wrong" (the victim's own realization). The user says "the slow realisation that something is wrong" — ambiguous whose realization. Could do the victim's: he feels off, blames the wine, then fear. Combining: mostly the detective's POV, but the realization sequence can render Voss's deterioration externally observed — or I could do a brief section from Voss's side. Mixed POV in one scene is risky for a novel chapter unless the user does that. Safer and very effective: single POV — the detective's — and let the "slow realization" happen through observed details plus the detective's own rising unease ("Something about the table had gone wrong, like a picture hung a degree off square"). Actually — many detective novels use the detective-as-witness to a poisoning (Sparkling Cyanide uses a group; Christie's "The Affair at the Bungalow"...). Detective as dinner witness works if I justify: she's at the hotel investigating something small (a theft? just eating?) or she's watching Voss already because he's a person of interest in another matter — that's a great justification: she's been quietly watching Voss for days over some business matter, so her observational habit is set up. I'll gesture at that lightly ("Voss, whom she'd been asked to look at... the commercial matter she didn't yet understand") without inventing too much plot the user didn't ask for. Keep it light: one clause hinting she has a reason to watch him.

Names final:
- Detective: Inspector... let me pick something Swiss/French: "Inspector Naomi Alder"? "Lena"? I'll use "Inspector Marguerite" no... Simplicity aids placeholder-ness: "Inspector Lanner"? I'll go with "Inspector Beatrice 'Bea' Amsel"? Hmm. Amsel = blackbird in German, nice. Or "Inspector Anna Brunner." Let me choose: Inspector Lena Amsel? Hmm, or maybe give the detective a distinctive habit (never drinks, eats the same thing, watches hands). A habit device: she watches hands — waiters' hands — professional habit. That motivates noticing the plate turn. I'll give her the habit of watching hands. Name: "Inspector Léonie Kader"? Keep it simple: Inspector "Lena Amsel"? Hmm — Actually maybe the user's detective already exists in their novel (chapters 1–8). I should write the scene with a placeholder name and say "swap in your detective." I'll choose "Inspector Adler"? Adler = eagle, common. Let me just pick "Inspector Lena Marchetti"? Geneva with an Italian-Swiss inspector is plausible (Ticino). Or a Genevan name: "Inspecteur Claude Antille" — Antille is a real Valais surname. I'll go with... decide: Inspector "Anna Keller"? Keller is common Swiss-German. Hmm, Geneva is francophone; police there would be "inspecteur." "Inspecteur Lena Keller" mixes fine — Geneva is diverse. Fine: Detective = Inspector Lena Keller. Hmm wait, I earlier considered waiter "K. Bronner/Keller" — avoid reusing Keller for waiter. Waiter = "Pavel"? Or give him a name via name tag: "his badge: F. MERCIER." A French name makes him less 'othered' — actually making the suspicious waiter a local French name avoids the cliché of the foreign waiter being sinister, and the suspicion falls on competence instead. Waiter = "Mercier"? But then he's subtly flagged... the user just needs a suspicious waiter. I'll name him via the maître d': "That's Mercier — new, this season." Hmm, or "Brandt." Decide: Waiter = "Mercier." Wait — Mercier is also a champagne brand ("Mercier" champagne!). That could be a cute irony or a distraction. Maybe pick "Ravanel"? "Devaux"? Devaux is also champagne. "Léger"? Léger means light — thematically cute (a light touch). Or "Perret," "Besson," "Vuilleumier." I'll go with "Perret." Hmm, or keep him nameless until after the collapse, when the maître d' says "Perret — he's been with us since April." Namelessness through the scene actually enhances suspicion: "the waiter" as a force. Then naming him humanizes ironically. Yes: nameless "the waiter" during the scene; named only at the end via maître d' ("Perret, madame. With us since the spring."). Nice beat.

- Victim: Konrad Voss? Or English industrialist "Sir..."? Geneva hotels hosted everyone. "Konrad Voss" — good. Wife: "Ilse Voss." Associate: "Dr. Meller" or "Herr Baumann." I'll use "Meller." Maybe wife + Meller + Voss = three. Give Meller one line of dialogue and nervous energy.

Hotel name: invent one — "Hôtel des Bergues" is real; invent: "Hôtel du Lac"? generic. "Le Beau-Rivage" is real (Hôtel Beau-Rivage Geneva — where Empress Sisi was killed! Fun resonance: actually Beau-Rivage Genève is where Empress Elisabeth was assassinated in 1898 — walking past to the boat. A detective novel in an old Geneva hotel can nod to that atmosphere). I'll invent "Hôtel Le Manoir du Lac"? Or "Hôtel Bellevue"? Real Bellevue exists. Invent "Hôtel des Trois Rois" — that's Basel (Les Trois Rois). Invent "Hôtel Le Rhône"? "Grand Hôtel du Quai"? I'll use "Hôtel Mont-Versan"? Hmm, invented elegant: "Hôtel de la Promenade." Or "Le Richemond" is real. Let me invent "Hôtel Le Sphinx"? no. "Hôtel Angleterre" is real (Angleterre & Résidence). I'll go with "Hôtel Beau-Séjour"? Hmm, Beau-Séjour is in Geneva? There is a "Hôtel Beau-Séjour" somewhere. To be safe, invent: "Hôtel Mirabeau"? exists in Geneva maybe. Honestly any plausible name risks colliding with something; fiction commonly uses invented-sounding names. I'll use "Hôtel des Palmes"? That's Palermo (famous). "Hôtel Le Léman" — Léman = Lake Geneva's proper name; plausible and evocative. Go: "Hôtel Léman" or "Le Léman." Fine.

Menu details for texture: lake fish — "féra" (Lake Geneva whitefish, palée/féra) — perfect local detail! The special: "filets de féra" — the waiter says the féra arrived this morning, one last portion... steering it to Voss. Then the plate turn happens with the féra. Soufflé? Dessert comes before collapse maybe, or collapse at the fish course. Timeline: aperitifs, wine, entrée, main (féra) — Voss collapses during/just after the main. Slow burn: he's off even before — the scene can seed earlier micro-symptoms? If poison is in the main, early symptoms come after. If in the aperitif, symptoms early. For "slow realization," better: symptoms creep during the main course — he thinks the room is warm; unsteady hand; wife thinks he's tired. The detective notices the plate turn right before/at serving. Then the collapse ~10 minutes later. Good pacing.

Other tension devices:
- Weather/heat: a warm evening, open windows to the lake, the jet d'eau — heat gives cover for symptoms ("the heat," everyone says).
- The detective dining alone with a book or notebook — classic observer pose.
- The maître d' hovering; the room half-full; a widow's table; an American couple — ambient texture but don't crowd it.
- Sound design: fan turning, cutlery, the lake's silence, a string trio or a gramophone? Era-flexible: "a pianist working through something Lisztian, unlistened to."
- The moment before collapse: Voss makes a joke; his wine glass knocks; the fork falls — small sounds betraying.
- The wife's realization: she sees his face change under the chandelier light; "Konrad?" — the name spoken twice, second time louder.
- Panic choreography: a dropped glass somewhere, the maître d' calling for a doctor, someone proposing brandy (classic fatal old remedy), someone saying "turn his head," the detective taking charge of the room quietly.
- The detective's action: stop the clearing ("No one touches this table."); order the doors? Maybe softer: she asks the maître d' to keep the kitchen staff in; she looks at the plate turned a quarter-rotation; she remembers.
- The waiter's tell: while chaos, he stands with his cloth folded; or he is the calmest; he says "I will bring water" and is incredibly efficient; his eyes go to the doctorless room; when the detective stops him from clearing, a pause — "Of course, madame" — too smooth; and the tiny thing: he removes Voss's wine glass anyway? No — detective stops all. Maybe his slip: he says "the doctor is coming" before anyone called? Ooh, that's a strong tell — how did he know a doctor was summoned? Someone might have said; but if rendered carefully it's chilling: "Shall I telephone for the doctor?" before anyone asked. Hmm, that's plausible-but-sinister. Or subtler: he anticipated — he'd already brought water/sugar? Let me not overstuff. Keep his tells: over-anticipation all evening (pouring before asked, the special steered to Voss, the plate turn), then post-collapse calm + attempt to clear + flat meeting of eyes.

Also "suspicion" should feel like misdirection potential — the waiter may be a red herring or the actual agent; leave open. The clue (turned plate) is physical evidence independent of the waiter's demeanor.

The detective noticing the clue — render in the moment: her habit of watching hands; she sees the plate set, then the wrist rotate it a quarter turn, "as if presenting it," done to no other plate; she thinks it's fussiness/aesthetics at the time — files it. Later: as chaos, her mind returns to it; she looks at the plate: the lemon/fish now facing... The narration can end with her crouched, looking at the plate from the angle Voss would have eaten — the arrangement of the food "as if composed for him." End line: something like "Someone had set that plate the way you set a table for a guest you knew precisely — the way you set it when the plate itself was the message." Hmm, maybe less florid: "He had turned the plate. Only his plate. She looked at the fish, arranged so neatly against the rim, and thought: everything on that plate faced Konrad Voss, and nothing faced her." Or end with the waiter's name reveal + her resolve: chapter hook.

Chapter-end hook options: (a) detective's realization line; (b) the waiter's calm exit and the detective's decision to find him gone — no, keep him present; (c) the wife screaming — too melodramatic for end; (d) detective pocketing the realization: "She had watched the whole dinner. She had seen everything. Now she had to work out what it was she'd seen." That's a nice detective-novel cadence.

Also, "the slow realisation that something is wrong" — I'll thread it in three beats: (1) Voss's small wrongnesses (heat, wine, joke trailing off), (2) the wife's pivot from irritation to fear, (3) the room's collective pivot (clink of the dropped fork, the maître d's voice going thin). Meanwhile the detective's unease starts *earlier* — before the collapse — because of the oddities; her stomach knows before her head. That's the tension: reader sees the waiter's oddities + detective's disquiet; readers know genre conventions: poison incoming. Dramatic irony established by the user's premise (they told readers victim is poisoned in ch. 9, presumably the blurb/preceding chapters set it). So the scene should reward foreknowledge: every ordinary detail doubles.

POV/tense: third person past, limited to the detective. The user may have first-person detective — I'll note they can re-voice. Keep sentences taut, sensory, restrained; avoid purple; allow a few strong images (the heat, the lake light going down, the waiter's stillness like a held breath). Genevan details: the lake, Mont Blanc in the last light, the fountain (Jet d'Eau — existed since 1891 in current form; fine), trams outside, lime trees on the quay, the hotel's brass and worn marble, a lift cage. Keep era loose (no cars/planes specifics; a telephone at the reception desk works for any pre-cell era; if their book is contemporary, "telephone for a doctor" still plausible in old hotel). I'll write it near-era-neutral with vintage texture; mention in the note they can adjust era and names.

Length/format: The scene itself maybe ~1,000–1,300 words. Then a brief "notes for you" section (short — maybe 4 bullets: the planted clue & payoff options; the waiter as suspect/red herring; names/placeholders; pacing tip for slow realization). The user explicitly asked for the scene; the notes are value-add for a novelist — keep tight so the response isn't bloated. Actually the user said "I don't need the chemistry, just the drama" — so don't lecture. A short craft note about where the clue is planted and how to pay it off is directly useful. Keep to ~5 lines.

Now draft the scene.

---

Opening: establish hotel, evening, heat, detective's position.

Draft:

Chapter Nine (title? Maybe just the scene. I could offer a chapter title like "The Last Féra"? or "Table Twenty-Two"? A small chapter title could delight. "The Last Portion" — nice, ties to waiter steering the special.)
